sections.h2: Selling a house in Franklin Township
sections.html:
Franklin Township is a large Somerset County township with no resale certificate of occupancy for home sales. That keeps the timeline short, since the fire inspection and the deed recording are the two fixed steps.

The township has an estimated 69,105 residents spread over 46.17 square miles of land. That is about 1,481 people per square mile at the 2020 count. For 2020 to 2024, 69.3% of homes are owner-occupied, the median home value is $457,900 and median gross rent is $2,115. Median household income is $124,648, and the mean commute to work is 33.5 minutes.

Franklin is a collection of villages that grew together, and buyers search by village name, so use the right one in your listing or when you talk to a cash buyer: Somerset, Franklin Park, East Franklin, Middlebush, Griggstown, Kingston, Six Mile Run, Pleasant Plains, East Millstone, Blackwells Mills or Weston.

sections.h2: Is a certificate of continued occupancy required?
sections.html:
No. The township's construction office confirms that a Certificate of Continued Occupancy inspection is not required when a residential home is sold. What is required is an inspection from the Fire Prevention Department, reachable at 732-873-2500, extension 6303.

That fire inspection is the state's smoke alarm, carbon monoxide alarm and portable extinguisher compliance check, and the township posts a smoke alarm application among its forms. Commercial sales are different: a commercial building or a new tenant needs a Certificate of Continued Building Compliance.

In practice, schedule the fire inspection as soon as you have a buyer, test every alarm yourself beforehand, and replace any that fail. Keep the passing result with your closing file so the buyer's attorney can see it. Skipping the resale certificate saves time, but it does not remove the need for open permits to be sorted out before closing.

Offices that touch a home sale in Franklin Township
OfficeWhat it handles
Construction CodeNo resale certificate of occupancy for a residential sale; permits and inspections for open work
Fire PreventionSmoke alarm, carbon monoxide alarm and extinguisher inspection before a residential sale
Clerk's OfficeRegistration of vacant and abandoned residential properties in foreclosure
Somerset County ClerkRecords the deed, with the realty transfer fee and GIT/REP form attached

Check two things: whether past work on the house was permitted, and whether the property sits in a historic district. Under the Uniform Construction Code, replacing roofs and siding on one- and two-family detached homes no longer requires a construction permit, with polypropylene siding as the exception.

That relief does not apply in a historic district. All siding and roof replacements there still need Historic Commission review and approval before work starts, and the township publishes a map of the districts.

  • Look at your last roof, siding, deck and basement jobs and confirm the paperwork exists.
  • Check the township's district map if you plan any exterior repair before selling.
  • Call the Construction Department at 732-873-7283, extension 6224, when you are unsure whether a job needed a permit.

Chapter 183 of the township code, amended by Ordinance 4393-23 effective March 26, 2023, covers vacant and abandoned residential properties in foreclosure. A mortgagee must inspect after filing a foreclosure complaint and register the property with the Township Clerk within 10 days. The nonrefundable annual fee is capped at $500.

The ordinance spells out what happens at transfer. When a covered property is sold, the owner is responsible for all code violations and must meet the Code Enforcement office within 45 days for a final courtesy inspection report. Failing to maintain a covered property can lead to a summons with a fine of up to $1,500.

If your house is headed toward foreclosure, selling before a complaint is filed avoids this registration track altogether. Ask the Clerk's Office whether your address already appears on the vacant property register.

sections.h2: How does the reduced transfer fee for seniors work?
sections.html:
New Jersey charges a lower realty transfer fee when the seller is a senior citizen, blind or disabled. About 18.3% of Franklin residents are 65 or older, so this schedule applies to many local sales.

For a price of $350,000 or less, the reduced rates are $0.50 per $500 on the first $150,000 and $1.25 per $500 on the portion from $150,000 to $350,000. Above $350,000, the schedule starts at $1.40 per $500 and climbs to $2.65 per $500 for the slice between $550,000 and $850,000.

A seller claiming the reduced schedule files the RTF-1 affidavit with the deed at the Somerset County Clerk's office. Have your closing attorney confirm that you qualify before you count on the lower figure.

A separate GIT/REP residency form travels with the deed as well. The person who signs the deed completes it, and a New Jersey resident uses the GIT/REP-3.

sections.h2: Roads and open space buyers care about
sections.html:
Buyers look at the school district, Interstate 287 and open space. Franklin Township Public Schools serve pre-K through grade 12 across 10 schools. Interstate 287 crosses the northern part of the township with two interchanges, and county routes 514, 518 and 527 carry local traffic. The New Jersey Turnpike lies just outside the township, with its closest interchanges two towns away in Edison, East Brunswick and Monroe.

  • Colonial Park, a 685.5-acre Somerset County park, includes the Arboretum, a rose garden and a golf course.
  • Six Mile Run Reservoir Site, a 3,037-acre state parcel, offers multi-use trails.
  • The Ten Mile Run Greenway covers 684 acres and runs over four miles in length.

The old Delaware and Raritan Canal towpath is now a state park along the northern and western edges of the township.

• A traditional listing works well for a house in good condition when you can wait on a buyer's financing.
  • A private sale suits an owner who already has a buyer and an attorney.
  • A cash offer fits a house with deferred repairs, an estate or a foreclosure notice, as long as the fire inspection is scheduled early.

Call Fire Prevention first, then set the closing date with the buyer's attorney. Bring the deed, your latest tax bill and any permit paperwork to the attorney, and confirm which GIT/REP form the signers need before closing.

faqs.q: Do I need a resale certificate of occupancy in Franklin Township?
faqs.a: No. The construction office confirms a Certificate of Continued Occupancy is not required for a residential sale. You still need the Fire Prevention Department's smoke alarm, carbon monoxide alarm and extinguisher inspection.

faqs.q: Who inspects smoke and carbon monoxide alarms before a Franklin Township sale?
faqs.a: The Fire Prevention Department. Its number is 732-873-2500, extension 6303, and the township posts a smoke alarm application among its fire prevention forms.

faqs.q: Can I replace my roof before selling without a permit in Franklin Township?
faqs.a: Usually yes for a one- or two-family detached home, since the Uniform Construction Code no longer requires a permit for roof replacement. A house in a historic district is the exception and needs Historic Commission approval first.

faqs.q: What is the senior citizen realty transfer fee in New Jersey?
faqs.a: It is a lower schedule for senior citizen, blind or disabled sellers. For prices up to $350,000 it is $0.50 per $500 on the first $150,000 and $1.25 per $500 on the portion up to $350,000, claimed on the RTF-1 affidavit.

faqs.q: What happens to a foreclosure property when it sells in Franklin Township?
faqs.a: The owner becomes responsible for all code violations at transfer and must meet the Code Enforcement office within 45 days for a courtesy inspection report. Mortgagees register covered properties with the Township Clerk within 10 days of their inspection.
